title: LinkedIn games analysis pipeline
text:
← Projects
This is a personal project to create a live analysis pipeline that will show descriptive analysis of daily LinkedIn games records between PM and CW.
This pipeline will serve to elucidate who is the better overall player in LinkedIn games (Tango, Zip, Pinpoint and Cross climb) to date; between players PM and CW. Beginning from April 29th till today, August 13, 2026, data will continually be updated manually in the raw .xlsx file and ran through the pipeline for analysis when rendered.
In addition to summarizing means, medians, standard deviations, and visualizing score distributions over time, this document also employs Bayesian independent‐samples t‐tests for each game type to quantify the strength of evidence for performance differences between PM and CW. In each case, Bayes factors (BF10) is computed along with prior and posterior distributions plotted to illustrate how observed data update our beliefs about any effect (see Note 1 below).
This document aims to describe, visualize, and evaluate, using both descriptive statistics and Bayesian hypothesis tests, to assess the differences in scores between the two players.
# Libraries utilized
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(car)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(BayesFactor)

# Load the data in
dat <- read_xlsx("LinkedIn_games_data.xlsx")
To account for missing data (e.g., failure to complete Pinpoint guesses), “-” will be recoded into N.A. and listwise deletion will be conducted to remove the data for the day. Additionally, since the data is manually entered, it is recorded in wide format. The code below pivots the wide format into long format, which is simpler for analysis.
Show the code
# Convert "-" into NA and all columns into double
dat <- dat %>% 
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ na_if(., "-"))) %>% 
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.double)) 

# Change to long format
dat_long <- dat %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -date,
    names_to = c("Player", "Game_type"),
    names_sep = "_",
    values_to = "value"
  )

text:
Bayesian Independent T-test comparisons
Here, using Bayesian Independent-samples t-tests, evidence for or against a difference in performance between PM and CW for each game type will be quantified. For each comparison, the Bayes factor (BF10) ia computed to measure the relative support for the alternative hypothesis (that the two players differ in average game scores) over the null hypothesis (no difference).
Additionally, prior (default) and posterior distributions of the standardized effect size will be calculated to assess how the observed data update beliefs under the default Cauchy prior (scale = 0.707)






Note 1: IMPORTANT NOTE



The subsequent analysis is made purely for fun. This is not a formalized statistics project, and even though Bayesian analysis is more robust to optional-stopping than frequentist methods, there are important considerations.

Continously re-running the analysis with the same default prior (Cauchy scale = 0.707) without formally updating it in light of past data can produce Bayes factors that are not strictly coherent under sequential updating.
Proper sequential analysis would require recalculating the posterior at each stage and using that as the new prior for the next stage. Here, the analysis always begins from the default prior, which may under or overestimate evidence until enough data have accumulated. Each Bayes Factor value should be regarded as snapshots of a formal sequentially updated analysis.

These results can only be used as informal visualization and intuitive understanding rather than confirmatory statistical proof.



Homogenity of Variance Assumptions
Runs Levene’s test as a check of homogenity of variance for each game type subsets. Although Bayesian t‐tests are typically robust to mild heterogeneity of variance, it remains good practice to understand whether this assumption might be violated.

Bayes Factor computation

Bayes factor computation for Tango between PM and CW.


Show the code
# Filter out PM’s values (remove NA from 'value')
tango_pm <- dat_longT %>%
  filter(Player == "PM", !is.na(value)) %>%
  pull(value)

# Filter out CW’s values (remove NA from 'value')
tango_cw <- dat_longT %>%
  filter(Player == "CW", !is.na(value)) %>%
  pull(value)

# Run Bayesian two-sample t-test
bf_obj_tango <- ttestBF(
  x = tango_pm,
  y = tango_cw,
  paired = FALSE
)

# extractBF() returns a data frame; the “bf” column is the numeric Bayes Factor
bf_tango <- extractBF(bf_obj_tango)$bf[1]

# Build a simple one‐row data.frame for kable()
data.frame(
  "Game Type" = "Tango",
  "BF10"      = round(bf_tango, 3),
  "Notes"     = if (bf_tango > 1) {
                   "Evidence favoring difference (H1)"
                 } else {
                   "Evidence favoring H0 or inconclusive"
                 }
) %>%
  # Display as HTML table with caption and styling
  kable(
    caption   = "Bayesian independent‐samples t‐test (Tango)",
    col.names = c("Game Type", "BF₁₀", "Notes"),
    format    = "html"
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(
    full_width        = FALSE,

# Obtain 10,000 posterior samples of the standardized effect size (delta)
posterior_samples_T <- posterior(bf_obj_tango, iterations = 10000)

# Convert to a data frame for easier handling
posterior_df_T <- as.data.frame(posterior_samples_T)

# Create a sequence of effect size (delta) values for the prior
delta_range_T <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 1000)  # reasonable range for visualization

# Compute the density of the default Cauchy prior (scale = 0.707)
prior_density_T <- dcauchy(delta_range_T, location = 0, scale = sqrt(2) / 2)

# Create a data frame for the prior distribution
prior_df_T <- data.frame(
  delta = delta_range_T,
  density = prior_density_T,
  Distribution = "Prior"
)

# Compute the density of the posterior samples
posterior_density_T <- density(posterior_df_T$delta, adjust = 1.5)  # adjust can be tuned for smoothing

posterior_df_density_T <- data.frame(
  delta = posterior_density_T$x,
  density = posterior_density_T$y,
  Distribution = "Posterior"
)

# Combine prior and posterior data frames
combined_df_T <- rbind(prior_df_T, posterior_df_density_T)

# Plot both distributions
ggplot(combined_df_T, aes(x = delta, y = density, color = Distribution, fill = Distribution)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.2, position = "identity") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Prior and Posterior Distributions of Effect Size (δ)",
    subtitle = "Tango: PM vs. CW",
    x = "Effect Size (δ)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Prior" = "#00CFC1", "Posterior" = "#FF6B5C")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Prior" = "#00CFC1", "Posterior" = "#FF6B5C")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
This document demonstrates a complete Bayesian analysis pipeline in R for a simple reaction time experiment with a 2×2 factorial design. The goal is to show, in a clear and reproducible way, how to move from a simulated dataset to a fitted Bayesian mixed-effects model, and then on to interpretation of the posterior, predictions, and basic hypothesis tests.
The focus here is practical. I assume you are comfortable with basic R, regression-type models, and the idea of random effects, but perhaps newer to Bayesian modelling with brms. Throughout, I explain the key Bayesian concepts that are directly relevant to the workflow, including priors, posterior distributions, mixed-effects modelling, and MCMC sampling.

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
Experimental Scenario
The example is grounded in a cognitive psychology setting. Imagine an experiment where participants respond to visual targets while two experimental factors are manipulated. The first factor is Viewing Condition, where participants either have a Restricted view or an Unrestricted view of some relevant aspect of the display. The second factor is Target Location, which can be Same or Different relative to a previous location.
The outcome of interest is reaction time (RT) in milliseconds. In line with typical inhibition-of-return paradigms, the data are simulated so that responses are slower when the target appears in the same location compared to a different one. The expected inhibition effect is around 20–30 ms. Viewing condition is not expected to have a strong effect, and there is no strong interaction between viewing condition and target location.

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
Setup and Data Generation
To begin, I load the necessary packages and set a seed for reproducibility. The main packages used are tidyverse for data handling, brms for the Bayesian modelling, bayestestR and bayesplot for working with the posterior, and tidybayes for tidy posterior extraction.

library(tidyverse) # Data wrangling and visualisation
library(brms) # Bayesian regression models (Stan backend)
library(bayestestR) # Posterior summaries and hypothesis tests
library(bayesplot) # Posterior visualisation tools
library(tidybayes) # Tidy extraction of posterior samples

set.seed(42)

Next, I create a trial-level dataset that reflects the 2×2 design and the expected pattern of means. 30 participants complete 24 trials per condition, producing a reasonably sized data set to resemble a modest laboratory sample.

# Parameters for simulation
n_subj   <- 30          # Number of participants
n_trials <- 24          # Trials per condition per participant

# Define cell means (ms), one row per condition so there's no risk of the
# means lining up with the wrong condition (expand.grid()'s row order isn't
# always what you'd guess - listing conditions explicitly avoids that trap)
# These values encode a ~25 ms inhibition effect for "Same" vs. "Different"
mu_table <- tribble(
  ~Viewing,       ~Location,    ~mean, ~sd,
  "Restricted",   "Same",         530,  30,
  "Restricted",   "Different",    505,  30,
  "Unrestricted", "Same",         525,  30,
  "Unrestricted", "Different",    500,  30
)

# Generate trial-level data
dat <- expand.grid(
  Subj     = 1:n_subj,
  Viewing  = c("Restricted", "Unrestricted"),
  Location = c("Same", "Different"),
  Trial    = 1:n_trials
) %>%
  left_join(mu_table, by = c("Viewing", "Location")) %>%
  mutate(
    RT      = rnorm(n(), mean = mean, sd = sd),
    Subj    = factor(Subj),
    Viewing = factor(Viewing, levels = c("Restricted", "Unrestricted")),
    Location = factor(Location, levels = c("Different", "Same"))
  ) %>%
  select(Subj, Viewing, Location, Trial, RT)

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
Priors
Before fitting, it’s worth being explicit about the priors. brms will pick default (flat or very weakly informative) priors automatically, but a Bayesian workflow is more transparent when priors are chosen deliberately. Here I use weakly informative priors centred on plausible values given the scale of the data (reaction times in the 400-600ms range, with an expected effect of a few tens of milliseconds):

Intercept: normal(500, 100) - centred on a plausible average RT, wide enough to not rule out much.
Fixed-effect coefficients (b): normal(0, 50) - centred on “no effect”, allowing effects up to roughly +/-100ms to be plausible a priori.
Residual and random-intercept SDs: exponential(1) - a standard weakly informative choice for scale parameters, keeping them positive and not too large.


priors <- c(
  prior(normal(500, 100), class = Intercept),
  prior(normal(0, 50),   class = b),
  prior(exponential(1),  class = sigma),
  prior(exponential(1),  class = sd)
)

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
Model fit

fit <- brm(
  formula = RT ~ Viewing * Location + (1 | Subj),
  data    = dat,
  family  = gaussian(),
  prior   = priors,
  chains  = 4,
  cores   = 4,
  iter    = 2000,
  warmup  = 1000,
  seed    = 42,
  backend = "rstan"
)

chains = 4 runs four independent MCMC chains so we can check they agree with each other (a key diagnostic for whether sampling has worked properly). warmup = 1000 discards the first 1000 iterations per chain while the sampler tunes itself, keeping the remaining 1000 per chain (4000 total) as usable posterior draws.

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:

Before trusting any of the results, we check that the chains converged. Rhat values close to 1.00 indicate the chains agree with each other, and Bulk_ESS/Tail_ESS indicate how many effectively independent draws we have.

Visualizing the posterior
The plot below shows the posterior distribution for each fixed-effect coefficient - essentially, how much belief the model places on each possible effect size after seeing the data.

tidybayes lets us extract the posterior draws for the effect we care most about - the difference in RT between the Same and Different location conditions (our simulated inhibition-of-return effect) - and plot its full distribution directly.

title: What we lose when we stop being able to tell
text:
Open with the claim, not the background. One short paragraph that tells the reader what the post argues, so they can decide in ten seconds whether to keep going. Assume they have not read anything else on this site.
Then the second paragraph does the setup — why the question matters, what the usual framing gets wrong. Prose runs at a 68-character measure and is justified, so paragraphs of three to six sentences sit better than very long or very short ones.

title: What we lose when we stop being able to tell
text:
The usual framing
Use ## for sections. Each one gets a hairline rule above it, which is what gives a long post its rhythm — so use them generously, roughly every three or four paragraphs, and give them real titles rather than “Background” or “Discussion”.
Inline formatting works as you’d expect: emphasis, strong, inline code, and a link. A footnote goes like this1 and collects at the bottom of the post.

A pull quote is a hairline on the left and larger type. Use one when a sentence is worth stopping on — not to break up text you think is boring.


A sub-point
### is available for a level below, though most posts don’t need it.

title: What we lose when we stop being able to tell
text:
Something worth flagging






NoteA note to one side



Callouts render as a hairline box with an accent rule on the left. .callout-note is the neutral one; .callout-warning, .callout-important and .callout-tip all work and look the same in this theme. Good for a methodological caveat or an aside that would derail the paragraph.

title: What we lose when we stop being able to tell
text:
Showing your work
If the post needs numbers, write the chunk and let it run — the output is framed automatically and the code block keeps its highlighting:

# Any R works here. Keep chunks short enough to read on screen.
summary(cars$speed)

    4.0    12.0    15.0    15.4    19.0    25.0 


Plots get a caption and are matted like a photograph. fig-cap writes the caption; fig-alt is the screen-reader description and is worth filling in:

plot(cars$speed, cars$dist,
     pch = 16, col = "#4b7a55",
     xlab = "Speed (mph)", ylab = "Stopping distance (ft)")

Refer to it in the text as Figure 1 and Quarto numbers and links it for you.
An ordinary image, if you want one without R:



A caption sits under the plate, left-aligned.

title: What we lose when we stop being able to tell
text:
Closing
Land the argument. One paragraph, no summary of what you just said — say the thing you were building toward, or the question you’re leaving open.

How to use this file
Copy the whole template-post/ folder, rename it to a slug (blog/detection-is-the-wrong-test/), replace the front matter and the body, and delete this last section. The folder name becomes the URL. Keep each post’s images inside its own folder so a post stays self-contained.

title: Example Post: Blogging Template
text:
Heading Structure
Quarto turns the title: field above into the page’s main heading automatically, so headings inside the post body should start one level down, at ## (not # - using # here would create a second, duplicate top-level heading).

## (H2) marks a major section of the post, like this one.
### (H3) marks a subsection within it, like the one directly below.

Quarto builds the page’s table of contents from these headings, so keeping them in order (H2 before H3, no skipped levels) keeps the TOC sensible.

A Subsection Example
This is what a subsection looks like - one level below the section it belongs to.

title: Example Post: Blogging Template
text:
Code Chunks
Code chunks use three backticks and curly braces naming the language, e.g. ```{r} or ```{python}. The #| lines at the top of a chunk are chunk options - settings for that one chunk only. Two of the most useful:

echo - whether the code itself is shown on the page (true) or hidden, showing only its output (false).
eval - whether the code actually runs when the site is rendered (true), or is just displayed as text without being executed (false). Useful for showing code that depends on something not guaranteed to be available at render time - a package, an API key, a large dataset - without breaking the build.


R example
This site’s other R pages (the LinkedIn games and Bayesian analysis projects) both use this same R engine, so this is the more “native” language for this site.

Python chunks work the same way, through the same R-based engine (via a package called reticulate that lets R call out to Python) - as long as the post’s front matter does not add a jupyter: python3 line. Setting eval: false here on purpose, just to demonstrate the option; remove it in a real post if you want the code to actually run.

title: What we lose when we stop being able to tell
text:
Open with the claim, not the background. One short paragraph that tells the reader what the post argues, so they can decide in ten seconds whether to keep going. Assume they have not read anything else on this site.
Then the second paragraph does the setup — why the question matters, what the usual framing gets wrong. Prose runs at a 68-character measure and is justified, so paragraphs of three to six sentences sit better than very long or very short ones.

title: What we lose when we stop being able to tell
text:
The usual framing
Use ## for sections. Each one gets a hairline rule above it, which is what gives a long post its rhythm — so use them generously, roughly every three or four paragraphs, and give them real titles rather than “Background” or “Discussion”.
Inline formatting works as you’d expect: emphasis, strong, inline code, and a link. A footnote goes like this1 and collects at the bottom of the post.

A pull quote is a hairline on the left and larger type. Use one when a sentence is worth stopping on — not to break up text you think is boring.


A sub-point
### is available for a level below, though most posts don’t need it.

Showing your work
If the post needs numbers, write the chunk and let it run — the output is framed automatically and the code block keeps its highlighting:

title: Simulation study: CLMM vs LMEM for 5-category ordinal outcomes
text:
1 Abstract
Ordinal outcomes with a small number of categories (e.g., 5-point Likert-type ratings) are common in psychology and cognitive science, yet they are routinely analysed with linear mixed-effects models (LMEM) that treat category scores as continuous, interval-scaled data. Cumulative link mixed models (CLMM) explicitly respect the ordinal, bounded nature of such outcomes, but it is unclear how much this matters in realistic repeated-measures designs with multiple between-subjects Likert-scored predictors. This simulation study, structured according to the ADEMP framework (Aims, Data-generating mechanisms, Estimands, Methods, Performance measures; Morris, White, & Crowther, 2019), compares CLMM and LMEM for a 5-category ordinal outcome with three between-subjects predictors (Group1, Group2, Group3) and one within-subject factor (Condition). Data are generated from a true cumulative logit mixed model containing only main effects, and both CLMM and LMEM are fitted with a Group x Condition interaction term to allow evaluation of Type I error alongside power. We vary distributional shape, intraclass correlation (ICC), effect size, and sample size. Performance is assessed via bias, empirical standard deviation, mean squared error, Type I error, power, and confidence interval coverage. Results are not yet available and will be inserted by the user after running the simulation locally.

title: Simulation study: CLMM vs LMEM for 5-category ordinal outcomes
text:
2 Introduction
Likert-type and other ordered-categorical response scales pervade psychological and cognitive science research: confidence ratings, agreement scales, symptom severity scores, and many experimental judgement tasks produce outcomes with a small, fixed number of ordered categories (often 5 or 7). Despite the ordinal nature of these data, it remains standard practice to code categories as consecutive integers and to analyse them with linear (mixed-effects) models, implicitly assuming equal spacing between categories and normally distributed, homoscedastic residuals (Liddell & Kruschke, 2018). This “metric” treatment of ordinal data can distort estimated effect sizes, inflate or deflate Type I error rates, and produce biased inferences, particularly when response distributions are skewed, polarised, or bounded near the scale limits (Bürkner & Vuorre, 2019; Liddell & Kruschke, 2018).
Cumulative link (mixed) models (CLMMs) provide a principled alternative: they model the probability of being in category k or below as a function of latent thresholds and a linear predictor, without assuming equal inter-category distances (McCullagh, 1980; Agresti, 2010). Extending this to hierarchical/repeated-measures designs, CLMMs incorporate participant- level random effects in the same way LMEMs do, but on the latent (logit or probit) scale rather than the observed integer scale (Christensen, 2022, ordinal package). Foundational and applied work on ordinal versus normal mixed models (e.g., Hedeker & Gibbons, 1994; Hedeker, 2008; Johnson, 2003) has long argued that treating ordinal data as continuous can bias inference, but direct, systematic comparisons in designs typical of psychology — repeated within-subject conditions crossed with multiple continuous/Likert-scored between-subjects predictors — remain relatively scarce.
This study addresses that gap using a Monte Carlo simulation designed according to the ADEMP framework (Morris, White, & Crowther, 2019), which structures simulation studies around explicit statements of Aims, Data-generating mechanisms, Estimands, Methods, and Performance measures. We simulate 5-category ordinal outcomes from a true cumulative logit mixed model with three between-subjects Likert-scored predictors and one within-subject factor, and compare CLMM and LMEM fits — each including a Group x Condition interaction term whose true value is zero — across variations in distributional shape, ICC, effect size, and sample size.

title: Simulation study: CLMM vs LMEM for 5-category ordinal outcomes
text:
3 Aims

Aim 1: How do CLMM and LMEM compare in terms of Type I error and power for detecting Group main effects and the Group x Condition interaction (whose true value is zero in the data-generating model)?
Aim 2: How does this comparison depend on distributional shape (symmetric vs skewed vs polarised), intraclass correlation (ICC), and sample size?
Aim 3: Does CLMM provide less biased estimates of fixed effects than LMEM when the true outcome is ordinal with 5 categories?

title: Simulation study: CLMM vs LMEM for 5-category ordinal outcomes
text:
4 Methods (ADEMP)
The simulation follows the ADEMP structure of Morris et al. (2019). Sub-sections below correspond to Data-generating mechanisms, Estimands, Methods of analysis, and Performance measures. All user-editable simulation values are isolated in a single chunk (Section 5) so nothing below needs hard-coded numbers changed by hand.

4.1 Data-generating mechanisms (D)
Data are generated from a cumulative logit (or probit) mixed model:
\[
\text{logit}\,P(Y_{it} \le k) = \alpha_k - \big(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Group1}_i + \beta_2 \text{Group2}_i + \beta_3 \text{Group3}_i + \beta_4 \text{Condition}_t + b_{0i} + b_{1i}\text{Condition}_t\big)
\]
for \(k = 1, \dots, 4\) thresholds separating \(K = 5\) ordered categories, with \(b_{0i}, b_{1i} \sim N(0, \Sigma)\) jointly normal participant-level random intercept and slope for Condition. Group1, Group2, and Group3 are participant-level, between-subjects predictors, each generated on a 1-5 Likert scale and (optionally) centered/standardised before entering the linear predictor. Condition is a within-subject factor with multiple levels. No Group x Condition interaction terms are included in the true DGM — all true interaction coefficients are zero — but both analysis models below still include a Group1:Condition interaction term so that its Type I error rate can be evaluated directly.
We vary:

Effect size for Group and Condition main effects (null vs small vs medium vs large, on the latent logit/probit scale).
Distributional shape, via the threshold set \(\alpha_1 < \dots <
\alpha_4\): symmetric, skewed, and polarised (extreme-heavy) category probability profiles.
ICC, via the random-intercept/slope variances and their correlation (low, medium, high).
Sample size (\(N\) participants), at least two levels.

The true interaction coefficient is fixed at zero across all scenarios.


4.2 Estimands (E)

Primary: \(\beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3\) (Group1/2/3 main effects on the latent scale), and the Group1:Condition interaction coefficient fitted by each analysis model (true value = 0).
Secondary: \(\beta_4\) (Condition main effect), thresholds \(\alpha_k\), random-effect variances/correlation, and implied ICC.



4.3 Methods of analysis (M)
For every simulated dataset we fit:

CLMM: ordinal::clmm(Y ~ Group1 + Group2 + Group3 + Condition + Group1:Condition + (1 + Condition | id), link = "logit") (switch link = "probit" to compare link functions). Wald z-tests are used for fixed-effect p-values (the default reported by clmm); an LRT alternative via anova() on nested models is noted in comments for users who prefer it.
LMEM: lme4::lmer(Ynum ~ Group1 + Group2 + Group3 + Condition + Group1:Condition + (1 + Condition | id)) on Ynum = as.numeric(Y), with Wald (or Satterthwaite/lmerTest, noted in comments) p-values.



4.4 Performance measures (P)
For each estimand, method, and scenario, across simulation repetitions we compute: bias, empirical SD, MSE, Type I error (for null effects, including the interaction), power (for non-null main effects), and 95% CI coverage, each with Monte Carlo standard errors (MCSE), following the formulae in Morris et al. (2019, Table 6).

title: Simulation study: CLMM vs LMEM for 5-category ordinal outcomes
text:
5 Simulation Parameters (User-Specified)


Code
# =============================================================================
# SIMULATION PARAMETERS -- USER SPECIFIED
# Edit the values below to match your own study. All downstream code
# references these objects; do NOT hard-code numbers elsewhere.
# =============================================================================

## --- Reproducibility -------------------------------------------------------
USER_SEED <- 20260819L  # random seed; change to your own preferred seed

## --- Sample sizes -----------------------------------------------------------
# Number of participants per scenario. Provide >= 2 levels to study how
# performance scales with N.
N_LEVELS <- c(100, 200)

## --- Within-subject Condition factor ----------------------------------------
N_CONDITION_LEVELS <- 4          # number of within-subject Condition levels
# Coding/spacing of Condition in the linear predictor. If TRUE, Condition is
# treated as a numeric/ordered variable with equally spaced scores
# (e.g., -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5 for 4 levels); if FALSE, Condition is entered
# as a factor with (e.g.) treatment/contrast coding -- edit CONDITION_CONTRASTS.
CONDITION_NUMERIC <- TRUE
CONDITION_SCORES  <- scale(seq_len(N_CONDITION_LEVELS), center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)[, 1]
# If CONDITION_NUMERIC == FALSE, specify a contrast matrix, e.g.:
# CONDITION_CONTRASTS <- contr.sum(N_CONDITION_LEVELS)

## --- Monte Carlo repetitions -------------------------------------------------
N_SIM_REPS <- 500   # simulation repetitions per scenario (increase to 1000+ for final runs)

## --- True fixed-effect values (latent logit/probit scale) -------------------
# Group1/Group2/Group3 main effects: null value (for Type I error) plus
# small/medium/large non-null values (for power). Edit magnitudes to reflect
# effect sizes plausible for your substantive area (these are placeholder
# defaults on the latent logistic scale, loosely following Cohen-like
# conventions rescaled for cumulative logit models).
BETA_GROUP_NULL   <- 0.00
BETA_GROUP_SMALL  <- 0.20
BETA_GROUP_MEDIUM <- 0.50
BETA_GROUP_LARGE  <- 0.80
BETA_GROUP_LEVELS <- c(null = BETA_GROUP_NULL, small = BETA_GROUP_SMALL,
                       medium = BETA_GROUP_MEDIUM, large = BETA_GROUP_LARGE)

# True Condition main effect (latent scale). Edit as needed; can also be
# varied across a vector of levels analogous to BETA_GROUP_LEVELS.
BETA_CONDITION <- 0.40

# True Group x Condition interaction is ALWAYS zero in the DGM (do not edit
# to a non-zero value -- this is required for the Type I error evaluation
# described in the Aims).
BETA_INTERACTION_TRUE <- 0.00

## --- Threshold sets (alpha_1..alpha_4) for K = 5 categories -----------------
# Each vector must be strictly increasing (4 thresholds for 5 categories).
# Symmetric: roughly equal mass across categories.
THRESH_SYMMETRIC <- c(-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5)
# Skewed: more mass concentrated in lower categories (positive skew in
# category counts); reverse signs/order for negative skew.
THRESH_SKEWED    <- c(-2.5, -1.0, 0.2, 1.2)
# Polarized: more mass at the extreme categories, little in the middle.
THRESH_POLARIZED <- c(-2.0, -0.3, 0.3, 2.0)

THRESHOLD_SETS <- list(
  symmetric = THRESH_SYMMETRIC,
  skewed    = THRESH_SKEWED,
  polarized = THRESH_POLARIZED
)

## --- Random-effects structure (participant intercept + Condition slope) -----
# SDs and correlation for low/medium/high ICC scenarios. Increasing the
# random-intercept SD relative to residual/latent-scale variance increases
# ICC; edit magnitudes to bracket the range plausible for your paradigm.
RANEF_SETTINGS <- tibble::tribble(
  ~icc_level, ~sd_intercept, ~sd_slope, ~cor_int_slope,
  "low",       0.5,           0.2,       0.0,
  "medium",    1.0,           0.3,       0.1,
  "high",      1.8,           0.4,       0.2
)

## --- Between-subjects Likert predictors (Group1/Group2/Group3) -------------
# Distribution used to generate each Group predictor on a 1-5 Likert scale.
# Options implemented below: "discrete_uniform" (equal probability 1-5) or
# "rounded_normal" (normal draw rounded and clipped to [1, 5]).
GROUP_GEN_METHOD <- "rounded_normal"   # "discrete_uniform" or "rounded_normal"
GROUP_NORMAL_MEAN <- 3      # midpoint of 1-5 scale, used if rounded_normal
GROUP_NORMAL_SD   <- 1      # spread, used if rounded_normal

# Whether to center (mean 0) and/or standardize (SD 1) Group1/2/3 before
# they enter the linear predictor. Centering is recommended at minimum so
# that beta_0 / thresholds retain a sensible reference (average participant).
GROUP_CENTER    <- TRUE
GROUP_STANDARDIZE <- FALSE

## --- Link function ----------------------------------------------------------
LINK_FUNCTION <- "logit"   # "logit" or "probit"; used both in DGM and in clmm()

## --- Derived / convenience objects (do not need editing) --------------------
set.seed(USER_SEED)



5.1 Helper functions


Code
#' Generate a 1-5 Likert-scale between-subjects predictor
#'
#' @param n number of participants
#' @param method "discrete_uniform" or "rounded_normal"
#' @param mean_ mean for rounded_normal method
#' @param sd_ sd for rounded_normal method
#' @return integer vector length n, values in 1:5
generate_likert_predictor <- function(n,
                                       method = GROUP_GEN_METHOD,
                                       mean_ = GROUP_NORMAL_MEAN,
                                       sd_ = GROUP_NORMAL_SD) {
  if (method == "discrete_uniform") {
    sample(1:5, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  } else if (method == "rounded_normal") {
    x <- round(rnorm(n, mean = mean_, sd = sd_))
    pmin(pmax(x, 1), 5)
  } else {
    stop("Unknown method for generate_likert_predictor()")
  }
}

#' Rescale a raw 1-5 predictor according to user preferences (center/standardize)
rescale_predictor <- function(x, center = GROUP_CENTER, standardize = GROUP_STANDARDIZE) {
  out <- x
  if (center) out <- out - mean(out)
  if (standardize) out <- out / sd(out)
  out
}

#' Simulate one dataset from the true CLMM data-generating model
#'
#' @param n_participants number of participants (N)
#' @param n_condition number of within-subject Condition levels
#' @param condition_scores numeric vector of Condition scores (length n_condition)
#' @param thresholds numeric vector of K-1 increasing thresholds
#' @param beta_group numeric vector length 3: true Group1/2/3 coefficients
#' @param beta_condition true Condition main-effect coefficient
#' @param beta_interaction true Group1:Condition interaction coefficient
#'   (should be 0 for all scenarios per study design)
#' @param sd_intercept random-intercept SD
#' @param sd_slope random Condition-slope SD
#' @param cor_int_slope correlation between random intercept and slope
#' @param link "logit" or "probit"
#' @return tibble, one row per observation (long format), columns:
#'   id, Group1, Group2, Group3, Condition (factor), Condition_num, Y (ordered
#'   factor), Ynum (numeric copy of Y)
simulate_clmm_data <- function(n_participants,
                                n_condition = N_CONDITION_LEVELS,
                                condition_scores = CONDITION_SCORES,
                                thresholds = THRESH_SYMMETRIC,
                                beta_group = c(0, 0, 0),
                                beta_condition = BETA_CONDITION,
                                beta_interaction = BETA_INTERACTION_TRUE,
                                sd_intercept = 1,
                                sd_slope = 0.3,
                                cor_int_slope = 0,
                                link = LINK_FUNCTION) {

  K <- length(thresholds) + 1

  # Participant-level between-subjects Likert predictors
  Group1 <- rescale_predictor(generate_likert_predictor(n_participants))
  Group2 <- rescale_predictor(generate_likert_predictor(n_participants))
  Group3 <- rescale_predictor(generate_likert_predictor(n_participants))

  # Correlated random intercept/slope via bivariate normal
  ranef_cov <- matrix(
    c(sd_intercept^2, cor_int_slope * sd_intercept * sd_slope,
      cor_int_slope * sd_intercept * sd_slope, sd_slope^2),
    nrow = 2
  )
  ranef_draws <- MASS::mvrnorm(n_participants, mu = c(0, 0), Sigma = ranef_cov)
  b0 <- ranef_draws[, 1]
  b1 <- ranef_draws[, 2]

  participant_df <- tibble(
    id = seq_len(n_participants),
    Group1 = Group1, Group2 = Group2, Group3 = Group3,
    b0 = b0, b1 = b1
  )

  # Expand to long format: one row per participant x Condition level
  long_df <- participant_df %>%
    tidyr::expand_grid(cond_index = seq_len(n_condition)) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      Condition_num = condition_scores[cond_index],
      Condition = factor(cond_index, labels = paste0("C", seq_len(n_condition)))
    ) %>%
    dplyr::arrange(id, cond_index)

  # Linear predictor (eta), NOTE: no true Group:Condition interaction term
  long_df <- long_df %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      eta = beta_group[1] * Group1 + beta_group[2] * Group2 + beta_group[3] * Group3 +
        beta_condition * Condition_num +
        beta_interaction * Group1 * Condition_num +  # kept for completeness; should be 0
        b0 + b1 * Condition_num
    )

  # Convert linear predictor into category probabilities via cumulative link
  link_fun    <- if (link == "probit") pnorm else plogis
  cum_probs <- sapply(thresholds, function(a) link_fun(a - long_df$eta))
  cum_probs <- cbind(cum_probs, 1)  # P(Y <= K) = 1
  cat_probs <- cbind(cum_probs[, 1], t(diff(t(cum_probs))))
  cat_probs[cat_probs < 0] <- 0
  cat_probs <- cat_probs / rowSums(cat_probs)

  y_draw <- apply(cat_probs, 1, function(p) sample.int(K, size = 1, prob = p))

  long_df %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      Y = factor(y_draw, levels = 1:K, ordered = TRUE),
      Ynum = as.numeric(y_draw)
    ) %>%
    dplyr::select(id, Group1, Group2, Group3, Condition, Condition_num, Y, Ynum)
}

#' Fit the CLMM analysis model to one simulated dataset
#'
#' Analysis model always includes the Group1:Condition interaction, even
#' though the true DGM has no interaction, so that Type I error for the
#' interaction term can be assessed. Fixed-effect inference uses Wald
#' z-tests as returned by summary(clmm_fit); see comment below for an LRT
#' alternative.
fit_clmm <- function(dat, link = LINK_FUNCTION) {
  fit <- tryCatch(
    ordinal::clmm(
      Y ~ Group1 + Group2 + Group3 + Condition_num + Group1:Condition_num +
        (1 + Condition_num | id),
      data = dat, link = link
    ),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (is.null(fit)) return(NULL)

  # Wald-based tidy summary (default). For an LRT alternative on a specific
  # term, fit a reduced model without that term and compare via anova():
  #   fit_reduced <- update(fit, . ~ . - Group1:Condition_num)
  #   anova(fit_reduced, fit)
  broom.mixed::tidy(fit, effects = "fixed") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(method = "CLMM")
}

#' Fit the LMEM analysis model to the numeric-coded version of the same data
fit_lmem <- function(dat) {
  fit <- tryCatch(
    lme4::lmer(
      Ynum ~ Group1 + Group2 + Group3 + Condition_num + Group1:Condition_num +
        (1 + Condition_num | id),
      data = dat, REML = TRUE
    ),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (is.null(fit)) return(NULL)

  # Wald p-values from lme4 by default (no df correction). For
  # Satterthwaite/Kenward-Roger df, refit with lmerTest::lmer() instead.
  broom.mixed::tidy(fit, effects = "fixed") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      p.value = 2 * pnorm(abs(statistic), lower.tail = FALSE),  # Wald z-approx
      method = "LMEM"
    )
}

5.3 Simulation run


Code
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# NOTE: This chunk can be slow (N_SIM_REPS x nrow(scenario_grid) model
# fits, each involving both a CLMM and an LMEM fit). Set eval: true only
# when ready to run the full simulation. For quicker iteration, reduce
# N_SIM_REPS temporarily, or parallelize with furrr::future_map_dfr()
# (commented alternative below).
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------

run_one_replicate <- function(scenario_row, rep_id) {
  dat <- simulate_clmm_data(
    n_participants   = scenario_row$N,
    thresholds       = scenario_row$thresholds[[1]],
    beta_group       = c(scenario_row$beta_group1, scenario_row$beta_group2, scenario_row$beta_group3),
    beta_condition   = BETA_CONDITION,
    beta_interaction = BETA_INTERACTION_TRUE,
    sd_intercept     = scenario_row$sd_intercept,
    sd_slope         = scenario_row$sd_slope,
    cor_int_slope    = scenario_row$cor_int_slope
  )

  clmm_est <- fit_clmm(dat)
  lmem_est <- fit_lmem(dat)

  dplyr::bind_rows(clmm_est, lmem_est) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(

5.4 Performance measure computation


Code
# True values for each estimand, keyed by scenario characteristics, used to
# compute bias / Type I error / power / coverage. Edit mapping if term names
# differ after tidy() (check unique(sim_results$term) first).
true_value_lookup <- function(term, group_effect) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    term == "Group1" ~ BETA_GROUP_LEVELS[group_effect],
    term == "Group2" ~ BETA_GROUP_LEVELS[group_effect],
    term == "Group3" ~ BETA_GROUP_LEVELS[group_effect],
    term == "Condition_num" ~ BETA_CONDITION,
    term == "Group1:Condition_num" ~ BETA_INTERACTION_TRUE,
    TRUE ~ NA_real_
  )
}

perf_summary <- sim_results %>%
  dplyr::filter(term %in% c("Group1", "Group2", "Group3",
                             "Condition_num", "Group1:Condition_num")) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    true_value = true_value_lookup(term, group_effect),
    is_null_true = near(true_value, 0),
    ci_lower = estimate - 1.96 * std.error,
    ci_upper = estimate + 1.96 * std.error,
    covered  = true_value >= ci_lower & true_value <= ci_upper,
    rejected = p.value < 0.05
  ) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(method, term, N, shape, icc_level, group_effect, true_value) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_reps      = dplyr::n(),
    bias        = mean(estimate - true_value, na.rm = TRUE),
    bias_mcse   = sd(estimate - true_value, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n_reps),
    emp_sd      = sd(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    mse         = mean((estimate - true_value)^2, na.rm = TRUE),
    mse_mcse    = sd((estimate - true_value)^2, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n_reps),
    reject_rate = mean(rejected, na.rm = TRUE),           # Type I error if true_value == 0, else power
    reject_mcse = sqrt(reject_rate * (1 - reject_rate) / n_reps),
    coverage    = mean(covered, na.rm = TRUE),
    coverage_mcse = sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / n_reps),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

7 Discussion
This section is a generic outline only; specific conclusions should be added once results are available.

When CLMM would be preferred: CLMMs are expected to show advantages over LMEMs particularly when the outcome distribution is skewed or polarised rather than symmetric, when the number of categories is small (as here, K = 5), and when effect sizes on the latent scale are moderate-to-large. Discuss whether the simulation supports this pattern.
When the two methods converge: Under symmetric distributions with many categories and low ICC, LMEM often approximates CLMM reasonably well; discuss whether this held here, and for which estimands (Group main effects vs the interaction Type I error) the two methods diverged most.
Practical recommendations: Provide guidance for applied researchers on choosing between CLMM and LMEM for 5-point Likert outcomes in repeated-measures designs with multiple between-subjects Likert-scored predictors, referencing the specific bias/power/Type I error patterns found.
Limitations: Note constraints such as the number of scenarios simulated, the specific random-effects structure assumed (random intercept + Condition slope only), the use of Wald-based inference for both models, and the restriction to a single true DGM form (cumulative logit with only main effects).
Future work: Extensions could include non-cumulative-logit DGMs (e.g., adjacent-category or continuation-ratio models), true non-zero interaction effects, model misspecification scenarios (e.g., fitting CLMM with the wrong link), and comparison against Bayesian ordinal models (e.g., via brms).
